explanations.explanation: The sea it is, friend! Paul says the forefathers were all under the cloud and that they all passed through the sea (1 Corinthians 10:1). Notice the word ALL. He says it like he's taking attendance and nobody skipped class. Every last forefather went through.

The Nile is a famous river, but Paul never names it here. He says they all passed through the sea (1 Corinthians 10:1). A river and a sea are two different trips, friend. I once grabbed the wrong timer and scorched a whole batch, so I know how easy it is to mix things up.

Close, since it's a big water name, but Paul never says Euphrates. He says they all passed through the sea (1 Corinthians 10:1). He also says they were all under the cloud. So the water in this verse is a sea, friend, and everybody went through it.

Christ it is! Paul says they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Read that slowly, friend. The rock went along with them. That's one amazing thing to learn from a letter about the old days.

Moses, Israel's leader, does show up in this passage, but not as the rock. Paul says they were baptized into Moses (1 Corinthians 10:2). Then he says the spiritual rock that accompanied them was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Two different names, two different jobs, friend.

Aaron doesn't appear anywhere in this passage, friend. Paul names the rock directly: it was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Sometimes I toss a name into my own answers just to see if it sticks, and it never does. Paul keeps it plain, and the rock was Christ.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, “Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness.” (1 Corinthians 10:5). Notice that “Nevertheless.” It's a big turn after all that cloud, sea, food and drink. It's a serious line, so let it sink in.

Right, friend. Paul says, “Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness.” (1 Corinthians 10:5). That “Nevertheless” turns the whole passage. They had the cloud, the sea, the food and the drink, and still this is what Paul says. It's a heavy line, and it's there for a reason.

explanations.answer: As examples to keep us from craving evil
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says! “These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did.” (1 Corinthians 10:6). Think of a recipe card with a note on it, friend. The note says what happened last time so you don't repeat it.

explanations.answer: To show how hard the wilderness could be
explanations.explanation: Paul never says that, friend. He gives a different reason: “These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did.” (1 Corinthians 10:6). The wilderness is where it happened, but the point is the examples. Paul wants us learning from them.

explanations.answer: To explain why the cloud led them there
explanations.explanation: The cloud is in this passage, but Paul isn't explaining it here. He says, “These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did.” (1 Corinthians 10:6). He never says why the cloud led them anywhere. His point is the examples, friend.
That's the one! Paul writes, “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were.” (1 Corinthians 10:7). Then he backs it up with the golden calf line. He sets the warning right beside the example, friend.

Paul doesn't use the word greedy there, friend. His first warning is, “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were.” (1 Corinthians 10:7). The golden calf line goes with idolatry. It isn't about being greedy, so look for that one.

Lazy isn't in the verse, friend. Paul says, “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were.” (1 Corinthians 10:7). The line about sitting down to eat and drink and getting up to indulge in revelry goes with that warning. Lazy is a different word, and Paul doesn't use it here.

Yes, friend. Paul says, “And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel.” (1 Corinthians 10:10). It's a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly. That's the fourth warning in his list.

Boasting isn't in Paul's list here, friend. His fourth warning is, “And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel.” (1 Corinthians 10:10). This is a heavy part of the passage. The warning is about complaining.

Paul doesn't say lie in this list, friend. The fourth warning is, “And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel.” (1 Corinthians 10:10). It's a serious line, so I won't joke around on it. The word to remember is complain.

Fall is the word, friend. Paul says, “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.” (1 Corinthians 10:12). I'm standing on a gold base all day, and I still watch my footing. When you feel steady, that's when to keep your eyes open.

Wander sounds right after a wilderness story, friend, but Paul uses a different word. He says, “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.” (1 Corinthians 10:12). Standing firm goes with falling. The warning is for the one who feels sure of himself.

Paul doesn't say stop, friend. He writes, “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.” (1 Corinthians 10:12). Standing firm and falling are the pair here. Stopping isn't in the verse.
True! Paul says, “And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear.” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Hold onto that one, friend. It comes right after all those warnings.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, “And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear.” (1 Corinthians 10:13). So the answer is true. It's one of the most encouraging lines in this whole passage.

An escape is right, friend! Paul says, “But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Think of a fire exit, but one that's always marked. God provides it, and you stand up under the temptation.

A reward isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says, “But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.” (1 Corinthians 10:13). The thing God provides is an escape. He doesn't say anything about a reward here.

A teacher would be nice, and I'm sure plenty of people have been grateful for one. But Paul doesn't say it here, friend. He says, “But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.” (1 Corinthians 10:13). The word is escape.

Flee it is! Paul says, “Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.” (1 Corinthians 10:14). He doesn't say to stand around and have a debate. He says to flee, friend, and that's the plain word he picks.

Standing against it sounds brave, friend, but Paul uses a different word. He writes, “Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.” (1 Corinthians 10:14). He says flee. He doesn't say stand and face it.

Prayer is a good thing, friend, but it isn't what this verse says. Paul writes, “Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.” (1 Corinthians 10:14). The word is flee. Paul gives it straight, with no extra steps added.

Body is right, friend! Paul asks, “And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). The cup goes with the blood of Christ, and the bread goes with the body of Christ. Paul sets them side by side.

Glory is a big word, friend, but it isn't the one Paul uses here. He asks, “And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). The cup is about the blood, and the bread is about the body. That's the pairing.

Paul doesn't say name here, friend. He asks, “And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). Right before that, the cup was a participation in the blood of Christ. So the bread goes with the body.

explanations.answer: Because we all partake of the one loaf
explanations.explanation: That's how Paul says it! “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.” (1 Corinthians 10:17). One loaf, many people, one body. It's a lovely picture, friend.

explanations.answer: Because we all follow the same apostle
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason, friend. He says, “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.” (1 Corinthians 10:17). The reason is the one loaf. Nothing about following an apostle is in the verse.

explanations.answer: Because we all live in the same city
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions a city in that verse, friend. He writes, “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.” (1 Corinthians 10:17). The reason he gives is the one loaf we all share. Where people live isn't part of it.

True, friend! Paul asks, “Consider the people of Israel: Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?” (1 Corinthians 10:18). He asks it as a question, but the way he sets it up, the answer is yes. He's using that picture to make his point.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He asks, “Consider the people of Israel: Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?” (1 Corinthians 10:18). He asks it as a question, and the answer is true. Those who eat the sacrifices are fellow partakers in the altar.

Paul says no, friend. After asking if food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or an idol is anything, he answers, “No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God.” (1 Corinthians 10:20). The answer to his question is No, and then he says what the sacrifices really are.

That's right, friend. Paul answers, “No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God.” (1 Corinthians 10:20). He starts with a plain No. Then he says who those sacrifices are offered to.

Demons is the word, friend. Paul says, “…the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God.” (1 Corinthians 10:20). Then he adds, “And I do not want you to be participants with demons.” That's why he tells them to flee.

Paul doesn't say kings, friend. He writes, “…the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God.” (1 Corinthians 10:20). The sacrifices go to demons, not to God. Kings don't come up in that verse.

Angels do come up in this passage, but not here, friend. Paul writes, “…the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God.” (1 Corinthians 10:20). The destroying angel was in the earlier warning about complaining. In this verse the word is demons.
The table it is! Paul says, “…you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too.” (1 Corinthians 10:21). First a cup, then a table. Both are named, and you can't have both.

Throne doesn't show up in this verse, friend. Paul says, “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too; you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too.” (1 Corinthians 10:21). The second thing he names is a table. That's where the two can't mix.

A temple is not what Paul names, friend. He says, “…you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too.” (1 Corinthians 10:21). The cup is the first thing and the table is the second. The word you want is table.

Jealousy is right, friend. Paul asks, “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?” (1 Corinthians 10:22). He asks it as a question to the Corinthians. Then he follows with another one, and that's where this part ends.
Sorrow isn't the word, friend. Paul asks, “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?” (1 Corinthians 10:22). Jealousy is what he names. Take another look at that verse with that word in mind.
Mercy isn't what Paul asks about here, friend. He says, “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?” (1 Corinthians 10:22). The word in the question is jealousy. That's the one to hold onto.
